book: Nutrition Through the Life Cycle (Brown), Chapter 14: Adolescent Nutrition and Chapter 15: Adolescent Nutrition: Conditions and Interventions
kicker: Lesson 8 of your course, built from Chapters 14 and 15 of your Nutrition Through the Life Cycle textbook. Test practice uses checked answers, because there is no official key for this test.

steps.title: What shapes how teens eat
teach: Three levels of influence shape teen eating. Personal factors include family and friends, food likes, role models, confidence and body changes. Environmental factors include home, school, fast-food places and stores. Macrosystem factors include how food is produced and sold, and the media and advertising. Good programs work on all three.
Snacks make up about a quarter of teens' daily energy and a large share of their added sugars. Soft drinks are the top source of energy and added sugar in teen diets.

act.prompt: Sort each influence into its level.

items.label: Friends' food choices
items.feedback: Peers are a personal or interpersonal influence.

items.label: What the school cafeteria sells
items.feedback: The school food environment is an environmental factor.

items.label: TV and online food ads
items.feedback: Mass media and advertising are macrosystem factors.

steps.title: Growth and key nutrients
teach: Adolescence is a time of fast growth. Teens hold on to more calcium than adults and build much of their lifetime bone mass, which is why calcium matters so much at this age. Milk and fortified drinks are key sources, and vitamin D helps calcium do its job.

Iron needs rise with fast growth, more blood volume and, for girls, the start of periods. Teens have the lowest folate levels of any age group, which matters for girls who could become pregnant. Breakfast cereals and orange juice help.

act.prompt: What is the best reason to make sure young teens get enough calcium?

options.label: They retain more calcium than adults and are building bone mass.
options.feedback: Yes. This is a key window for building bone.

options.label: They burn more energy in sports.
options.feedback: Energy use doesn't drive calcium needs.

steps.title: Talking with teens about food
teach: Teens respond to messages about the here and now, such as having energy for sports and friends, more than warnings about disease decades away. Focus on lasting healthy habits rather than short-term dieting.
A 24-hour recall, food frequency questionnaire or food record can all be used with teens. A 24-hour recall is quick to start in person and can easily be finished by phone later.

act.prompt: Which message is most likely to motivate a teen?

options.label: “Eating well will give you energy for sports and time with friends.”
options.feedback: Yes. Short-term, personal benefits work best with teens.

options.label: “Eating well may prevent heart disease later in life.”
options.feedback: Long-term disease risk feels far away to most teens.

options.label: “Eat it because it's good for you.”

steps.title: Overweight in adolescence
teach: For teens, BMI is compared with percentiles for age and sex. Between the 5th and 85th percentile is a healthy weight, the 85th to 95th is overweight (older guides say “at risk for overweight”), and the 95th and above is obese.
Up to 90% of overweight teens stay overweight as adults, so early support matters. Look at the share of Calories from fat when helping teens choose fast food: grams of fat × 9 ÷ Calories × 100.

act.prompt: A fast-food item has 500 Calories and 15 g of fat. What percent of its Calories come from fat?
act.explanation: 15 × 9 = 135 Calories from fat. 135 ÷ 500 × 100 = 27%, which is within 25–35%.

steps.title: Teen athletes
teach: Teens need energy for their basal metabolism, their activity and pubertal growth. Carbohydrates are the most effective way to build up muscle glycogen. Some endurance athletes use carbohydrate loading before a big event.

For fluids, drink about 16 oz for each pound lost during activity. During long events, sports drinks with no more than 6–8% carbohydrate, or juice diluted with water, hydrate better. Undiluted juice and stronger drinks can cause cramping.

act.prompt: A wrestler loses 2 lb during practice. How many ounces of fluid should he drink afterward?

steps.title: Eating disorders and special needs
teach: Binge-eating disorder means eating large amounts in a short time while feeling out of control, but without compensating by vomiting, laxatives or over-exercising. That last part is what sets it apart from bulimia. Treatment goals include a full diet assessment, a regular pattern of balanced meals, slowly bringing back “forbidden” foods, and stepping away from dieting and too much exercise. Family members can help by eating balanced meals themselves and showing love and praise that has nothing to do with food or weight.

Up to 40% of children and teens with special health care needs have nutrition risks that call for a referral to a dietitian. A lacto-vegetarian teen can get iron from beans and lentils, eaten with vitamin C foods such as tomatoes to boost absorption.

act.prompt: How does binge-eating disorder differ from bulimia?

options.label: It doesn't involve compensating behaviours like vomiting or laxatives.
options.feedback: Yes. That is the key difference.

options.label: It doesn't involve eating large amounts.
options.feedback: Both involve eating large amounts in a short time.

options.label: Binges are mostly fruit and vegetables.
options.feedback: The type of food isn't what defines it.

quiz.q: In order to improve the eating habits of youth, nutrition interventions should be aimed at three levels of influence. Which of the following would NOT be one of these levels?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The three levels are personal, environmental and macrosystem.

quiz.q: Snacks account for up to _____% of daily food intake among adolescents.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The textbook says snacks make up about one-quarter of teens' daily food energy.

quiz.q: The best reason for advising young adolescents to consume foods that provide adequate calcium is ____________________________________________________________________.
o: young adolescents expend more energy from increased physical activity and need more calcium
young adolescents do not have much money and dairy foods are the least expensive to buy
young adolescents retain four times as much calcium than adults and build bone mass
young adolescents fight with their parents a lot and this would eliminate one food battle
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Teens retain more calcium and build much of their bone mass.

quiz.q: All of the following are factors that increase a teen’s need for iron EXCEPT:
o: A rapid rate of linear growth.
The onset of menarche for females.
Greater intake of heme than nonheme iron sources.
All of the above factors increase a teen’s need for iron.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Heme iron is better absorbed, so it doesn't increase needs.

quiz.q: Susan is a 15-year-old who likes fruits, some vegetables, and breads (whole-grain and enriched) but refuses to consume milk, seafood, and eggs. A recent doctor visit revealed normal hemoglobin and plasma ferritin levels. What would you advise?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Her iron levels are normal and enriched breads give her folate, but without milk, seafood or eggs she has almost no vitamin D source. Health Canada, the AAP and the AAFP all recommend 400 IU of vitamin D a day for children and teens who don’t get enough from food.

quiz.q: An underweight 17-year-old male was 15 minutes late to his nutrition counseling appointment and he has to leave for a school-related practice in 20 minutes. What dietary assessment method would be the most appropriate for the dietitian to begin assessing his food intake pattern as well as a method that she could reliably complete on the telephone at a later time?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. A 24-hour recall is quick to start and easy to finish by phone.

quiz.q: Which of these messages is best for motivating adolescents to eat a healthy diet?
o: “Eating well will give you energy for sports or social activities.”
”Eat what you don’t like because it’s good for you.”
”Eating well may prevent heart disease in the long term.”
”Eat well now so you won’t be frail or disabled when you are old.”
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Teens respond best to short-term, personal benefits.

quiz.q: For which 16-year-old teen would the dietitian have the greatest concern about folate status?
o: Male whose estimated intake is 450 micrograms per day
Female who consumes orange juice and cereal for breakfast
Male with serum folate levels just below the normal range
Female who is sexually active and skips breakfast
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. She could become pregnant, and skipping breakfast means missing fortified cereal and juice.

quiz.q: Youth with body mass index (BMI) values > 50th percentile, but < 75th percentile are considered:
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Below the 85th percentile is a healthy weight.

quiz.q: As many as _____ of overweight adolescents can be expected to remain overweight into adulthood.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The textbook says as many as 90%.

quiz.q: Each pound of body weight lost during an activity requires ingestion of _____ ounces of fluid following the activity to maintain proper hydration.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The usual guide is 16 oz for each pound lost.

An adolescent is considering Tapango’s menu and would like to choose the food with the lowest percentage of fat calories. This would be the:
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Taco salad: 20.9 × 9 ÷ 502 = 37%. The others are 46–53%.

quiz.q: Would this food fit within the current recommendations for fat consumption?
o: No, it is high at 37% fat
No, it is high at 47% fat
No, it is low at 17% fat
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. 37% is above the 25–35% range for teens.

quiz.q: What beverage would be a good accompaniment to this meal and provide a nutrient that is usually scarce in adolescent diets?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Milk adds calcium, which is often low in teen diets.

quiz.q: A juice or sports drink that contains no more than _____ carbohydrate may allow for better hydration and physical performance than those that are more concentrated.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The textbook says no more than 6–8% carbohydrate.

quiz.q: A teenage girl ate Christmas dinner at her step-mother’s house and following a creamy dessert, announced, “I am fatter than all of my classmates; I am going to stop eating for 5 days!” Important behaviors the step-mother should model include all of the following EXCEPT:
o: eating well-balanced meals as part of her normal routine.
showing the step-daughter love without using food.
identifying strengths of the step-daughter that are not eating related.
beginning a subscription to Weight Watcher’s magazine for the stepdaughter.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. A dieting magazine would feed the focus on weight.

quiz.q: Binge-eating disorder differs from bulimia nervosa in that binge-eating disorder:
o: does not include binges on “fast” or “junk” foods.
does not involve eating large amounts of food in a short period of time.
does include large amounts of fruits and vegetables during a binge episode.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Binge-eating disorder has no vomiting, laxatives or other compensating behaviours.

quiz.q: Key goals of nutritional care for someone in treatment for an eating disorder would include:
o: establishing a regular pattern of nutritionally balanced meals.
gradually introducing forbidden foods into the diet.
avoiding dieting behaviors and excessive exercise.
thoroughly assessing dietary intake and adequacy.
All of the above are key goals
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. All four are goals of nutrition care for eating disorders.

quiz.q: An estimated _____ percent of children and adolescents with a chronic condition or disability also have nutrition risk factors that warrant a referral to a dietitian.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The textbook says as many as 40%.

quiz.q: What iron-rich food source would be the best choice for an adolescent who is a lactovegetarian?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Beans give iron, and the vitamin C in tomatoes helps absorb it. Lacto-vegetarians don't eat eggs or fish.
